name: Shambala
confidence_why: Every description of Shambala from Steere 1867 and Seidel 1895 through Odden 1982 (first-hand fieldwork) to Philippson 1991 and Mndeme & Ligembe 2022 places word stress on the penultimate syllable, realized as lengthening of that vowel rather than by pitch, and no source disagrees on placement or on the type of system.
sweep_summary: Shambala (sham1280) is in the catalog as fixed-dominant penultimate, decided by Steere 1867 ('The Accent in Shambala words invariably falls upon the last syllable but one'; quote re-verified, but the page is p.4 by the scanned page headers, not p.2). The two title-keyword items are both by Philippson: the 1991/92 Paris 5 thesis (Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique orientale) is a ~30-language comparative overview whose theses.fr abstract describes a continuum from tonal to demarcative-penultimate-stress systems and does not name Shambaa; it has no online full text (theses.fr 'accessible: non', no HAL, no OA PDF) - relevance unclear, priority medium. The 2005 paper (Pitch accent in Comorian and Proto-Sabaki tones, RMCA Tervuren volume) is about Comorian/Proto-Sabaki, not Shambaa (Seuta, G23): other-language, print-only, priority low. A side find, Philippson 1998 (Faits de Langues, Persée, doi 10.3406/flang.1998. Files already held by the project from the earlier catalog check were re-read: Odden 1982 SAL 13(2):179 gives the best first-hand statement - penultimate syllable stressed, realized as vowel lengthening with no pitch change - and supersedes Steere 1867 as deciding source; Seidel 1895 §4 p.1 ('Der Wortton ruht stets auf der vorletzten Silbe', stress shifts with suffixation, stressed open vowels long) and Riedel 2009 pp.17-20 (second-hand from Odden) confirm; Mndeme & Ligembe 2022 has a penultimate-vowel-lengthening rule but no stress statement. catalog's classification confirmed; deciding source should move to Odden 1982:179. lookups went through theses.fr, HAL, Semantic Scholar, Crossref, archive.

new_statements.quote: It should also be noted that the penultimate syllable of a word is stressed, realized phonetically as a lengthening of the penultimate vowel (but with no perceivable changes in pitch). A lengthened penultimate vowel is shorter than a long vowel, so the unstressed long vowel in ku-kaang-iy-a 'to fry for' is longer than the stressed vowel i. A stressed long vowel becomes even longer, so that the penultimate vowel in aa-ghook-a 'he is standing' is longer than the unstressed vowel aa.
new_statements.citation: Odden, David (1982). Tonal phenomena in KiShambaa. Studies in African Linguistics 13(2): 177-208.
new_statements.reading: Fixed penultimate word stress, cued by vowel duration (penultimate lengthening) and not by pitch; tone (H/L with downstep) is a separate system. First-hand 1981 field data from a native speaker (eastern dialect). Agrees with the catalog's fixed-dominant penultimate coding (rule_v3 penultimate stress) and with Seidel 1895 §4 and Steere 1867; adds the phonetic characterization and the stress/tone independence.

[pp.493-494]
new_statements.translation: c) languages with a culmination of length, but not of pitch, on the penultimate (languages with distinctive prosodemes but without a length opposition): Nande and Konzo; Langi; Nyanja and Chewa; Makonde; Shambaa, Bondei, Zigula, Ngulu; Mwani, Comorian, Pokomo, Mijikenda; Asu; Dabida and Saghala; Chaga; [p.483] || Group XVII: Shambaa: 1. [realized length opposition]: no; 2. [underlying length opposition]: yes; 3. [tonal or accentual system]: accentual language with H* melody; 4. [number of prosodic schemes of disyllabic nominal stems]: 5 [...] 10. [status of the penultimate syllable]: demarcative accent (culmination of length) [pp.508-509] || Shambaa is, as we have seen, exactly at the boundary between a tonal and an accentual language: although it has reached stage III and even set up a metrical-type structure heralding stage IV, it has reintroduced a series of prosodic oppositions in nominal stems, based mostly on the exploitation of downstep. [pp.493-494]

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog (penultimate stress = penultimate) and as Odden 1982 p.179 (penultimate stress realized as lengthening, not pitch). Adds: the accent is explicitly 'démarcatif' and cued by length only (class c, p.483); Shambaa lacks a realized length contrast but has an underlying one; the lexical H-tone system is treated as accentual (H* melody, marked syllables) and the language is placed at the tonal/accentual boundary (pp.493-494), whereas Odden treats it as tone; foot-structure constraint on H spreading (p.484). Data: author's own field notes (p.515) plus Roehl 1911, Kähler-Meyer 1962, Odden 1982 (bibliography p.524). Note: the listed open_url (theses.fr record) has no ful…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The penultimate syllable carries a demarcative accent realized as a culmination of length (not of pitch); Shambaa has no realized vowel-length opposition, so penultimate lengthening is the stress cue. Independently of this, the lexical H-tone system (five disyllabic and ten trisyllabic nominal schemes, pp.114-115; multiple association of H, pp.112-116) is analysed by Philippson as an accentual (H*-melody) system sitting at the exact boundary between tonal and accentual; the H-tone 'accent' is lexically placed and is not the penultimate demarcative accent.
new_statements.exceptions: None to the penultimate length accent. On the tone side: p.484 (d) I 'shambaa, bondei, zigula, mijikenda : un pied ne peut être entièrement compris dans les limites d'un mot que s'il débute avant la more (structurelle) pénultième de ce mot' (a H-tone foot fits inside a word only if it starts before the structural penultimate mora; otherwise the H spreads onto the next word, pp.113-116); p.114: taking the H marks as accentual would make Shambaa 'une langue à accent. Or, il ne semble pas, au premier abord, que les données confirment cette hypothèse'; p.116 fn.1 criticises Odden 1982 for positing two rules (disyllabic vs polysyllabic stems) instead of one.
new_statements.identity_note: Philippson's Shambaa data come from his own field notes (p.515), dialect not named, supplemented by Roehl 1911, Kähler-Meyer 1962 and Odden 1982 (p.524); Shambaa is classed G 23, groupe XVII (Seuta-Ruvu), marked '++' (well documented) in the sample table (p.72). Odden 1982 (existing statement) is eastern-dialect data. Roehl 1911 (not opened) is the Usambara mission grammar of the same language.

new_statements.quote: Betreffs der Betonung gelten folgende Regeln im Schambala: 1. Der Hauptton liegt in jedem Wort auf der vorletzten Silbe, die vielleicht aus diesem Grunde gewöhnlich lang ist, wie schon eben gesagt ist. 2. Ein Nebenton liegt bei Formen, die durch Affixe verlängert sind, auf der ersten Stammsilbe, die vielleicht auch infolge davon gewöhnlich lang bleibt. 3. Bei Formen, die durch mehrere Präfixe verlängert sind, liegt auf dem ersten Präfix ein Nebenton, der jedoch auf die Quantität des betreffenden Vokals ohne Einfluß bleibt. 4. Vor einsilbigen Worten rückt der Ton von der vorletzten Silbe des vorhergehenden Wortes auf die letzte Silbe desselben, wobei das einsilbige Wort seinen Ton verliert.
new_statements.translation: Regarding stress the following rules hold in Schambala: 1. The main stress lies in every word on the penultimate syllable, which perhaps for this reason is usually long, as just said. 2. In forms lengthened by affixes a secondary stress lies on the first stem syllable, which perhaps also as a result usually remains long. 3. In forms lengthened by several prefixes a secondary stress lies on the first prefix, which however has no influence on the quantity of the vowel concerned. 4. Before monosyllabic words the stress moves from the penultimate syllable of the preceding word onto its last syllable, the monosyllabic word losing its stress.
new_statements.citation: Roehl, Karl. 1911. Versuch einer systematischen Grammatik der Schambalasprache. (Abhandlungen des Hamburgischen Kolonialinstituts 2.) Hamburg: L. Friederichsen. xvi+214 pp.
new_statements.locator: Lautlehre, § 5 'Betonung', p. 5 (scan image 00000023; p. 16 of the copy consulted); supporting: § 4 'Quantität der Vokale', p. 5; § 6 'Der musikalische Ton', pp. 5-6; Tonlehre § 280 'Wortton', p. 198
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened the saved SUB Hamburg selection (39-page PDF, ionice -c3): the scanned with page marks at '[scan image 00000023 | p. 5]' and the text of p. 16 both carry par. 5, and I checked the rendered page scan printed p. 5, header '- 5 -') word for word. The quoted passage is there verbatim: 'S 5. Betreffs der Betonung gelten folgende Regeln im Schambala: 1. Der Hauptton liegt in jedem Wort auf der vorletzten Silbe, die vielleicht aus diesem Grunde gewoehnlich lang ist, wie schon eben gesagt ist. 2. Ein Nebenton.. auf der ersten Stammsilbe.. 3.. auf dem ersten Praefix ein Nebenton.. 4. Vor einsilbigen Worten rueckt der Ton von der vorletzten Silbe des vorhergehenden Wortes auf die letzte Silbe…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (fixed-dominant, penultimate stress = penultimate) and as Odden 1982 and Philippson 1991 (penultimate prominence realised as length, tone independent). Roehl adds: penultimate vowel length as the correlate already in 1911, two secondary-stress rules (first stem syllable; first prefix), the phrase-level shift to the final syllable before a stressless monosyllable with the exception of zé, and the explicit statement that musical tone is independent of dynamic stress and lexically contrastive.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary (dynamic) stress falls on the penultimate syllable of every word; the penult is the only regularly long syllable (§ 4: 'Lang sind nur die Vokale in der stets betonten vorletzten Silbe'), and a short vowel in the stressed syllable occurs mainly in loanwords (marked with a breve, e.g. ngŏda 'stick'). Musical tone (Hochton/Tiefton with half-high/half-low variants, §§ 6, 280-284) is a separate system, explicitly 'ganz unabhängig' of the dynamic stress and lexically distinctive (kiya 'water pot' vs kiya 'thigh' differing only in tone).
new_statements.secondary_stress: § 5.2: in affixally extended forms a Nebenton on the first stem syllable (which usually stays long, e.g. ōna 'see', ōnāna 'see each other'); § 5.3: in forms with several prefixes a Nebenton on the first prefix, without lengthening.
new_statements.exceptions: § 5.4: before a monosyllabic word the stress of the preceding word shifts from its penult to its final syllable and the monosyllable loses its stress (kúnu šī -> kunú šī 'here on earth'), without changing vowel quantity; the monosyllabic interrogative zé 'what? why?' is exempt and always keeps its own (weaker) stress, so the preceding word keeps penultimate stress (hámbu zé). § 4: loanwords may have a short vowel in the stressed penult (ngŏda).
new_statements.identity_note: Roehl describes the Schambala of East and West Usambara (Einleitung § 1, p. 1: 'Die Schambala wohnen in den schönen Bergen von Ost- und West-Usambara'), c. 100,000 speakers, worked out with the native assistant Eliza Cayuza (Vorrede p. X); no sub-dialect is singled out in the pages read.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on placement: Philippson 1991 (p.483 class c; Annexe p.509 rubric 10 'accent démarcatif (culmination de longueur)') puts the demarcative accent on the penult, realized by length and not pitch, exactly as Odden 1982 p.179 and the catalog's penultimate coding. The only divergence is analytic: Philippson labels Shambaa 'langue accentuelle à mélodie H*' and 'à la limite exacte entre langue tonale et accentuelle' (pp.493-494), treating the lexical H-tone marks as an accentual system, while Odden 1982 analyses the same facts as tone (H/L with downstep); this 'accent' is the lexically placed H, distinct from the penultimate length accent, so it does not contradict the stress record. Roehl 1911 could not be opened.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-dominant penult' rests on Steere 1867 p.2, a one-sentence remark in a missionary primer; we held no copy, but the archive.org text downloaded now confirms the sentence verbatim at p.2. The classification itself is safe: Odden 1982 (SAL 13.2, p.179), the standard phonological description of KiShambaa, states that the penultimate syllable of every word is stressed, realized as sub-phonemic lengthening (distinct from the marginal lexical length contrast) with no pitch correlate; Seidel 1895 p.1 says the same and adds that stress shifts with suffixation; Riedel 2009 and Mndeme & Ligembe 2022 repeat it; Hyman 2009/2013 (already held under other glottocodes) quote Odden 1999:192-3 to the same effect. Nothing found suggests exceptions or a non-penult pattern. Recommended: keep classification fixed-dominant/penult, swap or add Odden 1982:179 as the deciding citation (phonology article, fieldwork 1981)

A lengthened penultimate vowel is shorter than a long vowel, so the unstressed long vowel in ku-kaang-iy-a 'to fry for' is longer than the stressed vowel i. sources.locator: p.179, section 2 'Phonetic Problems' (scanned text; obvious scanned noise normalized)
sources.note: First-hand (1981 fieldwork, eastern dialect, speaker from Tanga): word stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable, realized as penultimate vowel lengthening with no perceptible pitch change; tone (H/L + downstep) is independent of stress. The paper also uses a [-stress] condition on object prefixes in its tonal rules (pp. ~194-198), i.e. stress is treated as a real phonological property.

He argues that this is expressed by lengthening the penultimate vowel, not by pitch raising." (second-hand, cites Odden)
sources.note: Second-hand (citing Odden 1982): regular penultimate stress realized as penultimate lengthening, not pitch raising.

sources.citation: Mndeme, Anuarite Samwel & Nestory Nyamwala Ligembe. 2022. Phonological Processes of Shambaa. International Journal of English Literature and Social Sciences 7(3): 41-61. doi:10.22161/ijels.73.8
sources.quote: Treats penultimate vowel lengthening (PVL) as a regular automatic process of Shambaa ordered after segmental rules; no separate stress statement. Low-tier journal, native-speaker fieldwork in Lushoto.
sources.note: Treats 'penultimate vowel lengthening (PVL)' as a regular Shambaa rule (e.g. /mioyo/ -> [myo:yo], /ndema/ -> [nde:ma]) but never states stress placement for Shambaa (its only 'penultimate stress' sentence is about English, citing Chomsky & Halle). Consistent with penultimate stress-as-lengthening; silent on stress itself.

sources.citation: Philippson, Gérard (1991 [theses.fr: 1992]). Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique orientale: étude comparative typologique et diachronique. Thèse de doctorat, Université Paris 5 (dir. Jacqueline M. C. Thomas), 542 pp. NNT 1992PA05H011.
sources.quote: We find a one end purely tonal systems (like kikuyu) and at the other end systems with purely demarcative penultimate stress, with all intermediate cases. [...] a hypothesis is presented according to which the emergence of penultimate accent is the main cause of the evolution of these systems. // FR: Une trentaine de langues en tout sont utilisées comme exemples. [...] l'émergence d'un accent démarcatif sur la pénultième servant de limite de domaine pour l'association tonale.
sources.locator: theses.fr record, FR and EN abstracts; field "accessible": "non"
sources.note: Comparative overview of the prosodic systems of ~30 East African Bantu languages, from purely tonal (Kikuyu) to purely demarcative penultimate stress (Swahili); argues the emergence of a demarcative penultimate accent drove the evolution of these systems. The abstract does not name Shambaa/G23, so whether it contains a Shambaa-specific stress statement could not be verified. No online full text: theses.fr marks it not accessible; no HAL record (author search, 16 records, none this thesis); Semantic Scholar record has no OA PDF; Print only (Sudoc holdings).

tone.quote: アクセントは通常表記されないが, この論文では, 音韻論的に見て高いと考えられる「拍」(単語のアクセントの記述において, どこが高くどこが低くどこがどうであるという際の「どこ」にあたるものの最小単位をこう呼ぶことにする。...)には(母音字もしくは鼻音字の上に)[´]を, 低いと考えられる拍には[`]を, 中くらいと考えられる拍には何もつけずに表記する。その他に, 同一拍の中で上昇すると考えられるものがあり, [ˇ]をつけて表記する。
tone.locator: pp.181-182, はじめに (introduction); tonal type labels (高高高高型, 低低高型, 高高高中型, 高高昇低型..) from the appendix pp.207-209
tone.translation: Accent is not normally written, but in this paper a 'mora' (the minimal unit referred to when one says, in describing a word's accent, which part is high, which is low and so on ...) that is judged phonologically high is marked with [an acute] (over the vowel or nasal letter), a mora judged low with [a grave], and a mora judged mid is written with no mark. In addition there are morae judged to rise within the one mora, and these are marked with [a hacek].
